item.description: On October 20, a monument to Alexander Solzhenitsyn was dismantled in central Vladivostok, where it had stood since 2015. It was supposed to be moved to a park commemorating victims of political repression, but the very next day it was unexpectedly put back. The official explanation was that it was too large for the new site. Vladivostok’s role in this story is no coincidence. It was there that Solzhenitsyn began his journey across Russia in 1994, after 20 years in exile. The writer traveled across the country to Moscow by train. After returning, he became active in politics, criticizing Gorbachev and Yeltsin but speaking favorably of Putin. The feeling is mutual: Putin honors Solzhenitsyn’s memory despite the writer’s views on the USSR and its suppression of dissent. At Meduza’s request, historian Alexey Uvarov explains how Solzhenitsyn’s contradictory views took shape — and how they foreshadowed the Russian-Ukrainian war.

item.title: Russia–Africa Summit: Moscow is engaging more with Africa, but its delivery is limited
item.description:
Russia–Africa Summit: Moscow is engaging more with Africa, but its delivery is limited Expert comment thilton.drupal 27 October 2026

Russia’s footprint in Africa has expanded in recent years, but engagement beyond security remains uneven. The summit alone is unlikely to change this.

The third Russia–Africa Summit, which was initially announced to take place in Libya, will now take place in Moscow on 28–29 October. The summit is being portrayed as a test of Russia’s growing influence across Africa. 

Once again, considerable emphasis is being placed on how many African leaders will be attending the gathering. The Kremlin says 22 African heads of state are attending, a slight increase on the 17 that attended the summit’s second edition in St Petersburg in 2023. That marked a significant decrease from the 43 leaders that were present at the inaugural summit in Sochi in 2019. Then, the Kremlin attributed the lower turnout to ‘outrageous’ Western pressure. 

Attendance at the summit, however, is a poor measure of durable partnerships. This is particularly the case as the constraints of Russia’s partnership have become harder for African governments to overlook. 

While Russian engagement with Africa has expanded in recent years, its economic delivery remains limited and the outcomes of its security role in the Sahel have been uneven. The summit may therefore lead to new agreements, but with the war in Ukraine still constraining Russia’s resources, it is unlikely to change these fundamental dynamics. 

Summit priorities

Russia’s interest in Africa reflects its own priorities. These include countering Western influence, building non-aligned partnerships and advancing multilateral reform. Expanding defence sales, securing minerals access and mitigating the impact of sanctions are also priorities. 

Moscow has pursued these objectives partly by using the BRICS grouping, which includes South Africa, Egypt and Ethiopia. It has also maintained its own bilateral political, security and economic relationships.

The summit, which will be accompanied by an economic and humanitarian forum, speaks directly to Moscow’s interests while also responding to African priorities. It is expected to promote new payment systems, reform of global financial institutions, stronger African representation at international organizations and opposition to unilateral sanctions. It will also discuss trade and investment, food and energy security, nuclear energy, technology and security cooperation. 

The summit is expected to produce a joint declaration, a separate declaration on AI cooperation, and an action plan for 2027–2029.

Russia’s deepening footprint

Security has been one of Russia’s main focuses in Africa. Since 2023, Africa Corps – the Russian state-controlled paramilitary force that replaced the Wagner Group – has expanded its presence. It has deployed beyond Mali, the Central African Republic and Libya to Burkina Faso and Niger. There are also reports pointing at possible deployments in Togo, which signed a military cooperation agreement with Moscow in 2025.

As insurgent attacks persist in the Sahel, Russia has deepened its ties with the Alliance of Sahel States (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger), pledging military and technical support. The three states have increasingly turned to Russia for security and diplomatic support following their break from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), and amid deteriorating relations with Western partners. Russia is also pursuing a parallel security cooperation agreement with ECOWAS, which will cover the broader region. 

Related work

Mali attacks show security cannot be delivered by military means alone

Diplomatically, Moscow has expanded its network of embassies on the continent, with planned missions bringing the total to 49. Russia has also sought to extend its diplomatic reach to the Horn of Africa amid rising tensions there, offering to mediate between Ethiopia and Eritrea on the margins of the summit in Moscow. The proposal signals Moscow’s ambition to position itself as a security interlocutor beyond the Sahel, although it remains an offer rather than a confirmed mediation effort.

Russia has also sought to deepen its economic footprint in Africa. Russian agricultural exports to Africa grew 35 percent in value in the first half of 2026, to $2.9 billion, with wheat shipments reaching record volumes. 

It has signed intergovernmental nuclear cooperation agreements with at least 15 African states.  For example, Rosatom, the Russian state nuclear corporation, signed an agreement to build a nuclear power plant in Ethiopia.   

Russia is also working with the African Union. At a July 2026 consultation in Addis Ababa, both sides committed to annual high-level political consultations and to launch sectoral dialogues. 

Limited returns

However, despite Russia’s deepening involvement in sectors such as energy and agricultural exports, trade between Africa and Russia is estimated at $27 billion in 2025, well below the $40 billion target announced by Putin in 2019.  It also pales in comparison to the EU’s €355 billion ($395 billon) and China’s $348 billion of recorded trade with Africa in 2025. 

In June, Russia’s foreign ministry acknowledged at a forum in St Petersburg that previous summits had produced more declaration than deals. It promised this third summit will be different.  

Related work

Can Africa maximize its global influence?

Agreements on nuclear power are yet to translate into completed projects. Egypt’s El Dabaa plant is still under construction. Ethiopia’s nuclear power plant is still at a prospective stage. 

Even in defence, the picture is not favourable. Russian global arms exports declined by 64 percent in 2021-2025. Russia ranked third, behind the US and China, in major arms supply to Africa during the same period. 

Russia’s increased security role in the Sahel has also failed to deliver reliable security guarantees. Annual deaths linked to violent extremism in the Sahel have increased from an average of 927 in 2016–2019 to an average of 10,470 in 2022–2025. 

In April 2026, a coalition of Tuareg separatists and al-Qaeda-linked jihadists killed Mali’s defence Minister and forced Africa Corps personnel to withdraw from the northern city of Kidal. Russian-backed forces subsequently regained control of Kidal in October, but the episode has exposed the limits of their security model. 

Russian-linked actors have sought to offset the costs of the war through security-for-resources arrangements, including control of and revenue from African gold mines; the US Treasury reports that gold and other African resources have helped Russia evade sanctions and fund its military efforts in Ukraine. 

There is also the question of the extent to which Russia can sustain its security commitments in Africa while its resources and attention remain stretched by the war in Ukraine.

Recruiting for the Ukraine war

Russia’s recruitment of African citizens to fight in Ukraine has become a reputational liability. A recent investigation cited by African media outlets estimated that more than 3,000 African citizens from 40 countries were recruited into Russia’s armed forces between October 2022 and June 2026, often through deception and promises of civilian jobs. Bloomberg reported this week that Moscow has been widening its recruitment drive in countries including Zimbabwe, Burundi and Sierra Leone. 

Related work

After Trump’s Russian diesel deal, will Europe give Ukraine the support it needs? 

African countries including Kenya and South Africa have sought to stop the recruitment of their citizens. During a visit to Moscow in April, Kenya’s foreign minister Musalia Mudavadi said that Moscow and Nairobi had agreed that Kenyan nationals would no longer be enlisted by Russia’s ministry of defence. Russia’s embassy in Nairobi had denied any involvement in recruitment.

An Afrobarometer survey of citizens across 38 African countries in 2024–2025 found that the perception of Russian influence was far less positive than that of China, the US, the EU and others, and 72 per cent of those who had heard of the Ukraine war wanted their country to remain neutral in it.

From rhetoric to delivery

The pattern of African engagement with Russia is best understood as diversified non-alignment. African governments see Moscow as one of several partners with whom they can pursue their interests in trade, security and greater representation in international forums. 

With Russia’s capacity constrained by the war in Ukraine, which continues to drain resources and diplomatic bandwidth, the real test is whether Moscow can convert political declarations and security interests into concrete, deliverable commitments in other fields.

Ultimately, Russia’s standing as a partner will depend on its ability to provide sustained economic benefits, reliable security partnerships and tangible outcomes for African countries. The summit will indicate the scale of Moscow’s ambitions; the years that follow will reveal how far it can realistically meet them.

item.title: The Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and Trump | Editorial
item.description:
If ever enacted, proposals by Marine Le Pen and the AfD leader, Alice Weidel, to hollow out EU institutions would be a continental act of self-harm

Following the Brexit referendum in 2016, Marine Le Pen was in a predictably celebratory mood. Britain’s vote to leave the European Union, she told one interviewer, was the first breach in the “Brussels Wall”. Ms Le Pen’s Front National party was at that point committed to taking France down the same path, given the chance. But as the UK’s self-inflicted economic wounds became a cautionary tale for the rest of Europe, the notion of Frexit was put on ice.

Instead, Ms Le Pen now hopes to lead far-right allies in hollowing out the EU from within. This month, both she and the leader of Alternative für Deutschland, Alice Weidel, outlined their visions of a “Europe of nations” in which EU institutions would be stripped of both cash and power. Ms Weidel’s “new deal for Europe” would abolish elections to the European parliament, and seek German opt-outs in areas such as migration, defence and common borrowing. Ms Le Pen’s party, now called National Rally, proposes slashing French contributions to the EU budget by 60% over a five-year presidential term, and ending the role of Brussels in proposing common policies for the 27 member states.

Bangladesh, Japan discuss $6.3b private investment in energy, infrastructure, ICT sectors
item.description:
Bangladesh and Japan today discussed a proposed private investment of 1 trillion Japanese yen (US$6.3 billion) in Bangladesh’s energy, infrastructure and information and communication technology (ICT) sectors during a bilateral summit between Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi.

The two leaders held the summit at the Kantei, the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office, at 11:30 am local time, where they also discussed sending a Japanese team to Bangladesh soon to expedite progress on the proposed investment plan, Prime Minister’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Shadhin told BSS.

The talks focused on strengthening the longstanding friendship between the two countries and expanding cooperation in trade, investment, energy security, technology, space research, infrastructure development and regional and international affairs.

During the meeting, Tarique Rahman called on the Japanese government and private sector to play a more active role in Bangladesh’s economic development, technological advancement and industrialisation.

Highlighting the government’s vision of transforming Bangladesh into a hub for economic activity, technology and manufacturing, the Prime Minister said the country could become the world’s ninth-largest consumer economy by 2030, while its gross domestic product (GDP) could exceed US$1 trillion by 2034.

He said Japan holds a special place in the hearts of the people of Bangladesh, recalling that it was among the first countries to recognise Bangladesh after its independence in 1971 and had since remained one of the country’s key development partners.

The relationship between the two countries, he said, was built on mutual respect, trust and shared aspirations for peace, prosperity and stability.
Emphasising Bangladesh’s energy security, Tarique Rahman said reliable and affordable energy supplies were essential to sustaining the country’s economic growth.

He expressed gratitude for Japan’s longstanding support in the energy sector and called for greater Japanese investment and participation in Bangladesh’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) infrastructure, efficient power generation and renewable energy.

Referring to a recent 50-billion-yen emergency assistance loan under the Partnership for Power Asia initiative to strengthen energy security in Asia, the prime minister highlighted opportunities to expand cooperation in the sector.

To help build a research- and technology-driven economy, Tarique Rahman proposed establishing a Bangladesh-Japan Tech Park to connect Japanese companies, universities and investors with Bangladesh’s young talent, entrepreneurs and skilled technology professionals.

He suggested prioritising artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, robotics and electronics manufacturing at the proposed facility.

The Prime Minister also expressed interest in expanding cooperation with Japan in space science, satellite engineering and related technologies, drawing on Japan’s advanced capabilities in these fields.

Highlighting the need for modern and integrated transport infrastructure, he outlined plans to establish a high-speed rail network connecting six major divisional cities and build elevated roads across the country.

He sought Japan’s cooperation in planning, providing technical assistance, investing in and financing such large-scale infrastructure projects.

Tarique Rahman said his government was committed to improving the investment climate through reforms to regulatory systems, tax policies, customs clearance and fund-transfer procedures.

He expressed hope that the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), signed in February 2026, would be implemented promptly.

He proposed establishing a joint ministerial commission to identify priority areas, accelerate implementation and translate opportunities for cooperation into concrete initiatives, while underscoring the importance of closer engagement between the two countries’ business communities.
The Bangladesh premier also invited Takaichi to visit Bangladesh at a mutually convenient time.

Following the summit, the two leaders made a joint press announcement on the outcomes of their discussions and exchanged several memorandums of understanding in key areas. Takaichi also hosted an official luncheon in honour of Tarique Rahman at the Kantei.

The Bangladesh premier arrived in Tokyo on Monday for a four-day official visit at the invitation of Takaichi. During the visit, he is also scheduled to deliver the keynote address at the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum and meet Japanese business leaders.

Dengue has claimed 11 more lives in Bangladesh in the past 24 hours, taking the death toll this year to 400. Of these, 155 people have died in the first 27 days of October alone, while 2,071 new patients have been hospitalised during the same period.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) disclosed the figures in its daily report on Tuesday.
According to the report, 899 of the newly hospitalised patients were from Dhaka division, the highest among the country's eight divisions. Khulna recorded 250 admissions, followed by Chittagong with 241, Rajshahi with 229, Barisal with 217, Rangpur with 112, Mymensingh with 97 and Sylhet with 26.
DGHS data show that dengue fatalities remained relatively low during the first five months of the year. Two people died in each of January and February, while no deaths were recorded in March or April. One person died in May.
The death toll rose to 13 in June, 36 in July and 43 in August before surging to 148 in September. In the first 27 days of October, the disease claimed another 155 lives.
September and October together accounted for 303 deaths, more than 75% of the year's total. By comparison, 97 people died of dengue in the first eight months of the year, highlighting a sharp rise in fatalities in recent months.
October's death toll has already surpassed September's total, with five days still remaining in the month.
Tuesday's report also recorded the highest number of dengue deaths in a single day this year, with 11 fatalities reported in the preceding 24 hours.
The previous highest daily toll was 10, recorded on October 6 and October 15.
According to the DGHS, a total of 128,237 dengue patients were hospitalised across the country between January 1 and 8:00am on October 27. Of them, 121,422 have recovered and been discharged, while 6,415 remain under treatment at hospitals nationwide.
The sharp rise in fatalities in September and October, coupled with the continued admission of thousands of patients, underscores the growing severity of the dengue outbreak across Bangladesh.
Medicine specialist Dr ABM Abdullah has stressed the need to destroy Aedes mosquito breeding sites and eliminate adult mosquitoes to curb dengue transmission.
He said the authorities should conduct regular cleanliness drives, while individuals must also take precautions to protect themselves from mosquito bites.
Some dengue patients are experiencing rapid deterioration, with some developing severe complications and going into shock within just one or two days, he said, urging people not to ignore a fever and to seek medical advice promptly.
Dr Abdullah advised extra caution if children, older people, pregnant women, and patients with cancer or liver disease develop a fever.
He also emphasised the importance of adequate fluid intake for dengue patients. Those experiencing vomiting, difficulty eating or diarrhoea should seek medical attention without delay.
He warned against taking painkillers purchased from pharmacies without consulting a doctor when experiencing a fever.
According to Dr Abdullah, early treatment improves the chances of recovery, while delays in seeking medical care can make severe cases, particularly those involving shock, more difficult to manage. Patients with underlying health conditions face additional risks, he added.
Dr Muhammad Nurul Islam, deputy director of Mugda Medical College Hospital, said people are exposed to different dengue virus variants each year. A second dengue infection could be one possible reason for the rapid deterioration in the condition of some children, he added.
He stressed that people should take dengue symptoms seriously even before the infection is confirmed. Patients should be closely monitored and take medication and undergo necessary tests as advised by a physician, he said.

item.title: Iran says supreme leader met with security chief over Hormuz
item.description:
Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has yet to appear in public since he took office in March, has met with security chief Mohsen Rezaei to discuss regional security and the Strait of Hormuz, his office said Tuesday.
Mojtaba was chosen in March to succeed his father and longtime ruler Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in US-Israeli strikes on February 28 in central Tehran alongside senior military commanders, and was said to have been injured in the same attack.
He has only communicated through written messages since his appointment, some of them published in handwriting attributed to him.
During the meeting, the first publicly announced encounter between Rezaei and the leader, they discussed “strengthening bilateral relations with neighboring countries” and “safeguarding national and regional security through the management of the Strait of Hormuz,” Khamenei’s office said in a statement.
Khamenei “emphasized the need to safeguard the rights and interests of the Iranian nation and the resistance front by adhering to the conditions set by the country’s authorities, with the aim of ending the war and the state of neither war nor peace,” it added.
Their meeting was announced a day after Rezaei held talks with senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan -- countries which recently signed the mutual defense Mecca Pact.
Neither the date nor the location of the meeting was disclosed.
Iran claims control over the Hormuz strait and regularly targets vessels that attempt to cross without its authorization, while the United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
Diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June deal which laid out a pathway to a permanent settlement.
Several Iranian officials, including Judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, have in recent days said they held rare meetings with the supreme leader.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,240 as 7 die in 24 hours
item.description:
Seven more children died with measles and measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours to 8am on Tuesday, bringing the country’s combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 1,240 this year.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified six latest fatalities as suspected measles deaths while another as a confirmed measles death.
With these, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,136, while confirmed deaths from measles stood at 105.
A total of 1,232 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, bringing the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 223,784.
Meanwhile, 63 new confirmed measles cases were recorded, bringing the total number of laboratory-confirmed infections to 23,541.
Since March 15 this year, a total of 199,127 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 191,090 have recovered, according to DGHS data.

item.title: IRRI, govt move to strengthen methane emissions monitoring in rice production
item.description:
The International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) has brought together government agencies, researchers and development partners in Dhaka for a two-day workshop aimed at strengthening Bangladesh’s capacity to measure, report and verify greenhouse gas emissions from rice cultivation.
The workshop, held on October 27–28, focuses on developing a national measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) system and advancing a methane mitigation roadmap for the rice sector.
Organized under the Accelerating the Scaling of Low-emissions Rice Production in Southeast Asia (AcceLER) project and CGIAR’s Climate Action and Scaling for Impact science programs, the event seeks to improve emissions tracking and institutional coordination.
Rice cultivation supports approximately 13 million farming households in Bangladesh but is also a major source of agricultural methane emissions.
Addressing the workshop, Agriculture Secretary Md Salim Khan emphasized the need to reduce emissions without compromising food security or farmers’ livelihoods.
“What we cannot measure, we cannot manage,” he said, adding that a transparent MRV system would strengthen Bangladesh’s greenhouse gas inventory and reporting under its Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), while creating opportunities for climate finance.
Department of Agricultural Extension Director General Md Abdur Rahim stressed the importance of reliable data systems for expanding climate-smart agricultural practices and accessing international climate finance.
Bangladesh Rice Research Institute Director General Dr Md Rafiqul Islam said the proposed MRV system must be cost-effective, scalable and transparent.
He identified alternate wetting and drying (AWD), climate-smart rice varieties, improved fertilizer management, direct-seeded rice and better residue management as potential measures to reduce emissions.
IRRI Bangladesh Country Representative Dr Humnath Bhandari highlighted the potential of digital MRV systems to provide reliable emissions data at farm, project and national levels.
IRRI Senior Scientist Dr Bjoern Ole Sander said research had identified practical approaches to reducing emissions from rice production, emphasizing methane’s contribution to global warming and ground-level ozone formation.
Technical discussions examined existing agricultural reporting systems, institutional responsibilities, data gaps and a proposed national MRV framework.
Participants also reviewed experiences from Cambodia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam in promoting low-emission rice cultivation.
The workshop includes practical greenhouse gas quantification exercises using IRRI tools, alongside discussions on remote sensing, digital data management and institutional requirements.
Organizers said the initiative aims to support Bangladesh in developing a coordinated, science-based system for monitoring agricultural emissions and implementing low-emission rice production practices.

item.title: HSC results delayed, new date set for October 31
item.description:
The results of this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations will be published on October 31, two days later than the previously announced date.
The Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee had earlier set October 29 for the publication of the results. The date was revised due to a change in the venue for the official result announcement.
Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee Chairman and Dhaka Education Board Chairman Professor Syed Akhtaruzzaman confirmed the decision on Tuesday.
He told Dhaka Tribune that the venue was changed following complaints from journalists about inadequate space at the Secretariat during last year’s result publication ceremony.
“Last year, journalists complained about the lack of space at the Secretariat on the day the results were published. We informed the education minister, who considered the matter and agreed to change the venue. Accordingly, the results will be formally published at the International Mother Language Institute on Saturday,” he said.
Earlier, the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee had proposed publishing the results between October 25 and 29. Based on the proposal, October 29 was initially fixed as the publication date.
The HSC and equivalent examinations under nine general education boards, the Bangladesh Technical Education Board and the Bangladesh Madrasah Education Board began across the country on July 2.
The exams were scheduled to end on August 8, but examinations under several boards, including the Chittagong Education Board, took longer to complete due to flooding.
A total of 12,70,583 candidates appeared for the HSC, Alim, HSC (BM-BMT), HSC (Vocational) and Diploma-in-Commerce examinations under 11 education boards. The exams were held at 2,697 centres involving 9,439 institutions.
This year, the nine general education boards conducted the examinations using common question papers.
The 2026 HSC and equivalent examinations began on July 2 and ended on August 8, while the practical examinations were completed by August 15.

item.title: UN: Greenhouse gas levels hit new record highs in 2025
item.description:
Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to new record highs in 2025, locking in climate impacts that will persist for centuries to come, the United Nations said Tuesday.
Levels of the three main greenhouse gases -- the climate-warming carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide -- all rose to unprecedented figures in 2025, the UN’s weather and climate agency said.
The World Meteorological Organization said the rise would lead to more long-term temperature increases for the planet.
The WMO’s 22nd annual Greenhouse Gas Bulletin comes ahead of the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, running from November 9 to 20.
“Another year, another new record,” said WMO deputy secretary-general Ko Barrett.
“Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies.
“The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. Carbon dioxide (CO2) has a very long life-time and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries.”
The bulletin looks at greenhouse gas concentrations -- the amount of those gases in the atmosphere -- rather than new annual emissions amounts as the world burns more coal, oil and gas.
In 2025, carbon dioxide concentrations were at 426.8 parts per million (ppm); methane at 1,948 parts per billion, and nitrous oxide at 339.1 parts per billion.
That takes them respectively to 153%, 267% and 126% of the pre-industrial levels witnessed before 1750.
Of the three major greenhouse gases, CO2 accounts for about 66 percent of the warming effect on the climate.
Around half of the total CO2 emitted each year remains in the atmosphere; the rest is absorbed by the land and oceans.
From 2024 to 2025, the global average concentration of CO2 rose by 2.8 ppm -- smaller than the record surge from 2023 to 2024 of 3.6 ppm.
WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova said this reflected the “recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Nino,” the naturally occurring, climate-warming weather phenomenon.
“However, a 2.8 ppm annual increase is still a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning.”
It is also above the average growth rate for the past decade of 2.6 ppm -- a figure that stood at 0.8 ppm in the 1960s.
“We can expect to see a further increase in concentrations in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and the development of a powerful El Nino which will impact land carbon sinks, as it did in 2023/2024,” Tarasova warned.
Methane accounts for about 16 percent of the warming effect on our climate by long-lived greenhouse gases, though it has a much shorter lifetime than CO2.
Around a third of methane emitted into the atmosphere comes from natural sources like wetlands, with the rest from anthropogenic sources such as cattle, rice farming, landfills and biomass burning.
The bulletin said that as countries shift their energy systems towards decarbonization, more attention should be paid to two potent but less abundant trace gases closely related to electricity production and distribution: molecular hydrogen (H2) and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6).
Primarily as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution, SF6 has been rising steadily over the past three decades.
Why H2 levels have increased over the past decade is unknown but it has begun to be used as an energy storage medium.

F-35 Fallacy: Jets Alone Will Not Save Us
item.description:
NATO Allies have bet the future of European skies on the world’s most sophisticated combat aircraft. NATO Allies are buying the world's most advanced fighter but many are neglecting vital investments in hard security, ground crews, and support systems that will keep it flying.

By 2028, European flight lines will host upwards of 700 F-35 Lightning jets. On paper, this inventory represents an insurmountable technological edge: a sensor-fused, fifth-generation fleet that outmatches any potential adversary in radar-cross-section, situational awareness, and electronic attack.

Yet this procurement spree masks a dangerous complacency. The Alliance has poured vast capital into acquiring fifth-generation airframes while systematically underinvesting in the unglamorous terrestrial infrastructure that keeps them flying: base hardening, counter-drone defenses, resilient networks, and ground crews. An F-35 sitting on an unhardened runway without fuel, parts, or secure command links is not a deterrent, it is an expensive target.

The cockpit may deliver tactical lethality, but operational endurance is generated entirely on the tarmac. If conflict erupts with Russia, the fight for European airspace will look less like a sterile, high-tech turkey shoot and more like the grueling attrition of the Battle of Britain.

Surviving Day Zero

Historically, the most efficient method of destroying an air force has rarely been in air-to-air combat; it has been catching it on the ramp. Operation Focus in 1967 wiped out Egypt’s air force before breakfast. Conversely, Ukraine averted immediate disaster in February 2022 because it aggressively dispersed its scarce aircraft and mobile air-defense batteries hours before Russian cruise missiles slammed into permanent garrisons.

Recent innovations have further collapsed the boundary between frontline and rear sanctuary. In June 2025, Ukraine demonstrated the democratization of deep strike with Operation Spiderweb, deploying commercial-style drones smuggled deep into the Russian interior to strike strategic bombers parked in the open. The threat bypassed layered air defense belts entirely; it originated outside the airbase perimeter fence. Coupled with intelligence reports of sabotage devices targeting logistical hubs in Western Europe, such as the attempted strikes near Leipzig, the implication for NATO is clear: rear sanctuary no longer exists.

Russia has studied these dynamics carefully. A coordinated "Day Zero" assault will not rely solely on long-range Iskander or Kalibr barrages. It will combine standoff salvos with covert proxy drone launches, special reconnaissance sabotage, and electromagnetic disruption targeting key airbases before any formal declaration of Article 5. If NATO’s F-35 fleet remains concentrated at sprawling, unhardened hubs, the Alliance risks losing the air war before its pilots can take off.

Survival on Day Zero will not come from a single system. Ground-based air defense will kill aircraft, cruise missiles will crater runways, and drones will hunt anything left in the open. The answer is dispersal, concealment, and resilience, practiced and exercised daily long before the shooting starts.

A Battle of Britain, Not a High-Tech War in the Air

The operational template NATO must internalize is not Desert Storm, but southern England in the summer of 1940. When the Luftwaffe hammered RAF sector stations across Kent and Sussex - cratering Biggin Hill, Manston, and Kenley - the British survived because of an integrated, highly resilient system.

It was not the Spitfire alone that preserved Britain; it was the Dowding System. Radar stations, visual observers, filter rooms, and telephone lines fused intelligence into an actionable operational picture and directed scarce interceptors to precise intercept vectors. Crucially, the system was distributed and made redundant. When individual nodes went dark, the architecture adapted. Meanwhile, exhausted ground crews patched runways and re-armed aircraft under constant threat of bombardment.

NATO faces an analogous network challenge today. The F-35 is a formidable intelligence-collection platform, but its utility plummets if its Multifunction Advanced Data Link (MADL) cannot pass target tracks to legacy fourth-generation fighters, naval surface combatants, or ground-based air defenses under heavy electronic jamming. If a Combined Air Operations Center (CAOC) is knocked offline, who assumes control of the theater airspace? Without distributed, jam-resistant data architectures and mission command protocols for degraded environments, tactical technological dominance will dissolve into operational paralysis.

Operational Imperatives for NATO Airpower

If NATO intends to build genuine deterrence by denial, member states must balance platform acquisition with systemic survivability across five core areas:

  1. Institutionalize Dispersal and Agile Combat Employment (ACE): Finland and Sweden have long mastered highway-strip operations, rapid turnaround, and camouflage doctrine. These must cease to be High North novelties and become standard operating procedure across all Allied air forces. Peacetime operations must routinely exercise dispersed sortie generation from municipal airports and road networks.
  2. Harden the Perimeter and the Flight Line: Every euro invested in advanced airframes must be matched by funding for base survivability: point-defense against low-altitude UAS, hardened aircraft shelters, mobile arrestor gear, rapid airfield damage repair (RADR) kits, and deep magazines of precision munitions.
  3. Expand Logistics at Strategic Depth: Dispersed operating locations demand rapid logistics and robust aerial refueling capacity. Staging fighters farther from the contact line requires a dramatic expansion of NATO’s multinational tanker fleet and hardened pipeline distribution networks.
  4. Solve the Cross-Domain Data Mesh: Allies must field resilient, low-probability-of-intercept gateways that translate fifth-generation sensor data into common operational pictures accessible to non-stealth assets and ground-based integrated air and missile defense systems. They also need the ability to protect and secure their entire EW spectrum, given the F-35's massive reliance on it.
  5. Re-arm and Re-train the Ground Crew: The maintainer, armorer, and combat engineer are frontline combatants. NATO must equip ground personnel with specialized force-protection capabilities, chemical-biological-radiological-nuclear defense gear, and the cross-training required to generate combat sorties in austere, contested conditions.

The True Cost of Deterrence

Deterrence is not measured by the sophistication of one platform; it is measured by the credible ability to absorb a first strike and generate combat power under fire. Building that credibility requires realistic, high-tempo exercises in harsh weather, degraded communications environments, and austere road bases. It must be under conditions that carry legitimate operational risk and wear on equipment.

Before 1989, this operational friction was the routine cost of doing business in Allied Air Forces Central Europe. The pilots of 1940 earned their place in history, but unheralded mechanics, plotters, and engineers preserved their freedom to fight. As NATO retools for contested collective defense, it must remember that fifth-generation air power is only as resilient as the ground beneath its wheels.

item.title: Division between Iraq’s Kurdish parties risks undermining Kurdistan region’s autonomy
item.description:
Division between Iraq’s Kurdish parties risks undermining Kurdistan region’s autonomy Expert comment jon.wallace 28 October 2026

The KDP and PUK largely agree on Kurdish issues in Turkey, Iran and Syria. But division on how to govern at home could invite outside interference and undermine hard-won self-governance.

Two years after Iraq’s Kurdistan Region went to the polls to elect a new government, the KDP and the PUK – the region’s two largest parties – have still failed to reach an agreement to form the new government. A caretaker government, originally elected in September 2018, remains in charge.

This situation is taking the Kurdistan Region down a path of profound and possibly permanent division. Its longstanding partners in Europe and the US have grown frustrated with its latent dysfunction and are no longer willing to play referee. This leaves it more vulnerable to interference from regional powers who are better placed to adapt and can play a longer game.

The main impediment to moving forward is not petty disagreements between the two parties over ministerial positions, as is sometimes claimed. Instead, the impasse stems from the collapse of the 2006 Strategic Agreement between the KDP and the PUK. The parties no longer share the same basic vision for how the Kurdistan Region should operate. The formal and informal frameworks that bound the two parties together for the last two decades are no longer functioning.

Instead, the Kurdistan Region has effectively divided into two geographic areas that are controlled by one party or the other. The KDP is in charge in Erbil and Duhok governorates. The PUK is dominant in Sulaymaniyah and Halabja.

The two zones are not fully separate, as they were during the era of divided administrations between 1998 and 2005. But it is a cumbersome arrangement. State institutions and the security forces look to unelected party leaders for guidance, not Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) ministries. Reports indicate that rents are extracted from truckers and traders at checkpoints on the border between KDP and PUK areas.

Until now, the parties have maintained that the Kurdistan Region remains a cohesive entity despite the partisan divide. On 6 October, KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani called on the parties to reactivate Kurdistan’s Parliament, which has not had a substantive meeting in more than four years saying: ‘I don’t know what they are afraid of’.

Below the surface, however, bigger changes may be afoot.

Hear directly from the experts

Get nuanced insights from Chatham House experts on the issues shaping the global policy and geopolitical landscape.

Political leaders from the PUK have a more radical proposal: to devolve administrative and fiscal authority to governorates, mayors, and district directors. Some powers would be retained by the KRG and the Kurdistan Parliament. But most important decisions over everyday matters would be shifted to lower levels of governance. Proponents of the plan cite Switzerland’s cantons and the UAE’s emirates as inspiration. Better to get out of each other’s way, the argument goes, and disaggregate executive authority.

Given the outsized power wielded – exclusively and separately – by the two parties at the governorate and local levels, this change would formalize partisan control over governance within the Kurdistan Region’s two zones, representing the biggest constitutional change in a generation. 

And it would repudiate the key peacebuilding assumption following the Kurdish civil war: that strong, unitary, and shared institutions are needed to reinforce Kurdish self-government and autonomy. That it is even being considered reflects the depths to which relations between the KDP and the PUK have deteriorated.

Many parts of the plan are vague. How would it change the relationship between local authorities, the federal government, and the KRG? How will revenues be shared, if at all? How will decisions be made about key sectors like oil, gas, electricity, and trade?

For the moment this remains a PUK proposal, its prospects uncertain. The KDP opposes the plan – part of the reason there has been little progress in negotiations to form a government. Many Kurdish voters will oppose reinforcing the power of the ruling parties without any meaningful checks. And, while they are certainly disillusioned by their present circumstances, they are keenly aware of the risks the PUK plan would pose to the Kurdistan Region’s fragile constitutional position in Iraq.

Over the past five years, Iraq’s federal government has gradually eroded the KRG’s ability to manage its own political and economic affairs, enabled by the KDP and the PUK disunity. 

A bad time for division

The potential for a fracture inside the Kurdistan Region comes at an inopportune time geopolitically. The US–Iran War has created significant instability. Foreign partners are preoccupied with problems at home. And changing regional dynamics are seeing sovereign states reassert influence over non-state actors.

The US presence in the Kurdistan Region is less potent than in years past. It completed a military withdrawal at the end of September after twelve years as part of the international coalition fighting Islamic State. Diplomatic activity in Erbil – where the KRG is based – has been hampered for much of this year due to security concerns stemming from the US–Iran war.

American and European diplomats are discouraged by their inability to bring the KDP and the PUK together, despite restlessly encouraging them to form a government. This inability is a signal of the West’s flagging influence over top Kurdish leaders. That will only worsen if diplomats have to contend with empowered local officials that answer primarily to the KDP and the PUK leadership.

The Kurdistan Region’s immediate neighbours like Turkey and Iran are much better placed to adapt to a Kurdistan Region that is divided and disaggregated. They can play the long game, and act at the local level through economic, social, and religious ties, rather than the top-down military and political approach of the US and Europe. Unity between the KDP and the PUK matters far less in their calculations.

Turkey’s immediate aim in the Kurdistan Region is to ensure that its own Kurdish political process, which is seeing the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) disarm, continues. The KDP and the PUK have strongly supported this process and provided important interventions to facilitate it. They have also supported the integration process of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into the new Syrian state. 

In the near-term, the KDP and the PUK are unlikely to diverge much from this path. But the risk is that greater division at home could fragment their positions on issues beyond the Kurdistan Region’s borders. If that happens, Ankara might side with one of the parties, which would result in further instability.

Iran’s first goal is to ensure that Kurdish groups do not enter its war with the US. So far, the KDP and the PUK are in lockstep about the importance of avoiding any impression that they might intervene against Iran. Tehran’s second goal is to curtail the activities of its own Kurdish armed groups, even to the point of demanding they be expelled from Iraq’s Kurdistan Region. Weak and divided state institutions in the KRG make this difficult to achieve. That, in turn, makes it more likely that Iran will take matters into its own hands.

In the absence of a US security presence, interference from regional neighbours could also lead Iraqi leaders in Baghdad to become more hands-on in dealing with matters in the Kurdistan Region. This would be a bad outcome for Kurdish self-governance and would likely inflame political tensions between the KDP and the PUK.

The sour mood that prevailed in the Kurdistan Region during the election two years ago has only deepened. Pushing governance decisions to the local level in an effort to avoid intractable partisan impasse at the top is one proposal. But it could have significant knock-on effects.  

A continued impasse between the KDP and the PUK risks setting off an irreversible decline for the frameworks that have enabled Kurdish self-governance for the past two decades. To get beyond this blockage, leaders from the KDP and the PUK must entertain imaginative solutions, but not ones that further divide, weaken its shared institutions or undermine democratic principles. Otherwise, it risks becoming a place that other actors pick apart at the expense of Kurdish autonomy.

item.title: Trump is in a corner and likely to lash out at Iran again. Here’s how to avert that disaster | Simon Tisdall
item.description:
Once the midterms are over, Trump will be free to pursue vendetta politics. But with will and diplomacy, he can be reined in

As another Iran catastrophe looms, one question matters more than any other: how to stop it before it’s too late? Whatever the eventual outcome of Israel’s election and next week’s US midterm polls, Donald Trump, playing the Lone Ranger, and Benjamin Netanyahu, his badass Tonto, appear hell-bent on resuming the illegal war of choice they began in June last year and expanded in February. Like a Shakespearean tragedy moving inexorably to a bloody denouement, the worst is yet to come. And yet three things seem certain: the US and Israel will again fail to totally destroy Iran’s largely hypothetical nuclear capabilities; its regime will survive; and millions of ordinary people, there and around the world, will pay the price for this unjustified, reckless aggression.

Ducking and weaving, Trump is desperate to dodge the blame for the Republicans’ anticipated midterm meltdown, largely triggered by war-related fuel and consumer price inflation. He claimed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries were responsible, but that didn’t wash. He cut a treacherous diesel deal with Vladimir Putin but, as usual, Russia’s smirking mafioso conned him. He urged US allies to tap their strategic reserves but, unsurprisingly, vilified and sidelined European leaders, who view his war as an unmitigated disaster and declined to bail him out. Trump also reportedly rebuffed last-gasp, electorally driven pressure from Netanyahu to hit Iran this month, fearful it would unleash a Democratic tsunami.
